title: What Factor Investing Is And How The Strategy Works?
summary: Factor investing picks shares by a trait such as momentum, value, quality or low volatility. See how factor index funds work and why momentum can fall hard.
body_markdown:
Factor investing means choosing shares by a trait that can be measured, using fixed rules, rather than by company size alone or a manager's judgement. The trait might be how far a price has risen lately, how cheap a company looks, or how profitable it is. In India it comes as index funds and ETFs that follow a published factor index, and as some actively managed funds.


## What is factor investing?


Factor investing is picking shares by a measurable trait, which the industry calls a factor. An ordinary index, such as the Nifty 50, is a list of companies chosen by fixed rules, and its value is tracked every day. Larger companies get larger weights. A factor index works differently. It starts from a broad index, such as the Nifty 200 or the Nifty 100, and keeps the companies that score highest on one trait.


An index fund is a mutual fund that holds the shares of an index in the same proportion as the index does. An ETF is the same thing, except its units are listed and traded on a stock exchange. For more on how the two differ, read[ETF or index fund](https://koshex.com/blog/etf-vs-index-fund) . For index basics, see[active vs passive funds](https://koshex.com/blog/active-vs-passive-mutual-funds-know-the-difference) .


SEBI's rules require an index fund or ETF to hold at least 95% of its assets in the securities of the index it tracks. After the index changes, the fund must rebalance within 7 calendar days. Rebalancing means adjusting the holdings to match the new list.


So a factor index is a rulebook, not a forecast. The fund follows the rulebook. Nobody is promising the rulebook will win.


## What are the main factors?


The factor indices most used by Indian funds pick stocks by momentum, value, quality or low volatility. Volatility means how sharply a price swings. Here is what each NSE index measures, going by the index provider's published methodology.


Index What it measures Stocks Reshuffled


Nifty200 Momentum 30 Price rise over 6 and 12 months, adjusted for volatility 30 from the Nifty 200 June and December


Nifty200 Value 30 Earnings, book value and sales relative to price, plus dividend yield 30 from the Nifty 200 June and December


Nifty200 Quality 30 High return on equity, low debt and steady earnings growth over 5 years 30 from the Nifty 200 June and December


Nifty100 Low Volatility 30 Smallest price swings over the past year 30 from the Nifty 100 Every quarter


In plain words, Momentum 30 takes the 30 Nifty 200 stocks whose prices have risen most over 6 and 12 months. It allows for how bumpy the ride was. Value 30 takes the cheapest on earnings, book value, sales and dividends. Dividend yield is a share's yearly dividend divided by its price.


Quality 30 takes firms with high return on equity, low debt and steady earnings. Low Volatility 30 takes the 30 Nifty 100 stocks whose prices moved least over the past year. For how a price's swings are measured, see[how to measure a mutual fund's risk](https://koshex.com/blog/5-ways-to-measure-mutual-fund-risk) .


The momentum, value and quality indices cap each stock's weight at no more than 5%. Low Volatility 30 weights stocks by how little they swing, and caps thinly traded ones at 3%.


### Can an index mix factors?


Yes. NSE Indices also publishes multi-factor indices. Its Alpha Low-Volatility 30 mixes two traits. NSE says multi-factor indices aim "to counter the cyclicality of single factor index strategy". That is the index provider's description of its design, not a promise of returns.


### Is company size a factor too?


Yes. SEBI's large cap, mid cap and small cap categories are built on it. Ranks 1 to 100 by full market capitalisation are large cap, 101 to 250 are mid cap, and 251 onwards are small cap. Market capitalisation is a company's share price times its number of shares. See[small cap funds](https://koshex.com/mutual-funds/categories/small-cap-funds) .


SEBI also has active categories named after value and dividend yield. They are not factor indices. They are covered on[value and contra funds](https://koshex.com/mutual-funds/categories/value-and-contra-funds) and[dividend yield funds](https://koshex.com/mutual-funds/categories/dividend-yield-funds) .


## What is a smart beta fund?


"Smart beta" is the industry's name for an index fund or ETF whose index picks stocks by a factor rule, not plain size. SEBI's master circular does not use the term. Where it mentions momentum, volatility and quality, it calls them "factors". That is in the rules that keep such factors out of the schemes a diversified equity[fund of funds](https://koshex.com/blog/etf-vs-fof) invests in.


A smart beta fund faces the same fee ceiling as any index fund or ETF. An open-ended one may charge a base expense ratio of at most 0.90% of daily net assets. The expense ratio is the fund's yearly fee, shown as a percentage of your money. Brokerage, exchange levies and statutory levies sit outside that base ratio.


There is a second cost. Each reshuffle means buying and selling shares inside the fund. Those trading costs come out of the fund's value, on top of its fee.


Tracking error is how far a fund's returns drift from its index. For a fund that is not a debt fund, SEBI says it shall not exceed 2%, and funds disclose it daily.


## What are momentum funds, and why can they fall hard?


A momentum fund holds shares whose prices rose most over the past 6 and 12 months, and it can fall further than the market. The Nifty200 Momentum 30 index scores each stock on those two returns, each adjusted for how bumpy its price was. It keeps the top 30 and reshuffles in June and December.


Here is a dated example. These are index figures, not any fund's result. From 27 September 2024 to 7 April 2025, the Nifty200 Momentum 30 fell 31.8%. The Nifty 200, the index it picks from, fell 17.2% over the same dates.


**Illustration on index figures, not a fund's result.** Say ₹1,00,000 had moved exactly with each index between those two dates. With the Nifty200 Momentum 30 it would have fallen to about ₹68,210. With the Nifty 200 it would have fallen to about ₹82,800. Both are price indices, so the figures leave out costs and tax.


The fall had not been made up by 30 September 2026. On that day the momentum index closed 22.6% below its 27 September 2024 close. Past falls do not predict future ones, and this one says nothing about the next.


Active momentum funds exist too. They are filed as thematic equity funds, and a manager runs the strategy.


## Is factor investing active or passive?


It can be either. An index fund or ETF tracks a published factor index, which is the passive kind. Some actively managed thematic funds run a momentum, quality or quant strategy, which is the active kind.


The fund's name and its AMFI heading tell them apart. A tracker is listed as an index fund or an ETF, and its name carries the index. An active factor fund sits under the equity sectoral or thematic headings. See[sectoral and thematic funds](https://koshex.com/mutual-funds/categories/sectoral-thematic-funds) .


Even the passive kind makes a bet. It follows an index, not a manager's choices, but the index itself backs one trait. So it is passive in how it is run and active in what it bets on. For the ETF side, see[exchange traded funds](https://koshex.com/blog/exchange-traded-funds) .


## Does factor investing work?


No one can promise that a factor will do better than the broad market, and past results are no forecast. What can be shown is dated: the momentum fall above, almost twice that of the Nifty 200 over the same dates.


NSE Indices itself describes single-factor strategies as cyclical, in the wording quoted above.


SEBI makes every fund show a riskometer, a label with six levels from Low to Very High, checked every month. On 29 September 2026, almost every listed index fund read Very High.


So read a factor fund as a rule that backs one trait.


## What should you check before buying a factor fund?


Check which index the fund tracks, or which strategy an active fund follows, because that rulebook is the fund. Then look at the rest.


- **The index and its method.** NSE Indices publishes the methodology for each index.
- **How often it reshuffles.** Every six months for momentum, value and quality; every quarter for low volatility.
- **The expense ratio and tracking error.** Each reshuffle adds trading costs inside the fund.
- **The riskometer.** Read it for the fund, not for the idea.
- **Overlap with what you hold.** Check how much of a new fund repeats funds you already own. See[mutual fund diversification](https://koshex.com/blog/mutual-fund-diversification) .
- **Your time frame.** A fall of 31.8% over about six months is hard to sit through if the money is needed soon.


An index fund on a factor index of Indian shares meets the 65% test, so it is taxed as an equity fund. Gains on units sold within 12 months are taxed at 20%. Gains on units held for more than 12 months are taxed at 12.5% above ₹1,25,000 in a tax year. A SEBI-registered mutual fund's own income is exempt, so trades inside the fund create no tax for you. Details are in[how SIP returns are taxed](https://koshex.com/blog/how-sip-returns-are-taxed) .
